chicken-wing-baked-or-broiled-from-pre-c.title: Chicken wing, baked or broiled, from pre‑cooked

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken wings are small pieces of poultry meat that are typically baked or broiled. In this case they are pre‑cooked (pre‑boiled, seasoned and cooled), allowing quick reheating in the oven or on a grill without further cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wings are a staple in American cuisine, especially for "Buffalo wings".
Pre‑cooked wings can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or frozen for up to 3 months.
Baking without added oil retains most of the flavor while keeping the dish lower in fat.
Wings are rich in collagen, which may support joint and skin health.
Various sauces—from sweet‑spicy to creamy—are paired with wings around the world.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken wings provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Wings supply iron, zinc, and phosphorus important for blood health and bones.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Makes them suitable for low‑carb dietary patterns.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and moderate fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Pre‑cooked wings are often salted; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Risk of over‑consumption
items.content: Flavorful sauces and seasonings can lead to eating more than the recommended portion.

items.title: Proper reheating
items.content: When reheating, ensure the internal temperature reaches at least 74 °C to prevent foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat the wings in a 180 °C oven for 10‑15 minutes or quickly broil them on a grill. Serve with your favorite sauces, vegetable sticks, or a salad. Adding extra spices before reheating can boost flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in a zip‑lock bag at –18 °C, where they retain quality for up to 3 months. Always reheat thoroughly before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg Burrito with Bacon is a breakfast dish consisting of a soft wheat tortilla wrapped around scrambled eggs, fried bacon, cheese, vegetables, and sometimes salsa. It is popular in Mexican and American cuisine as a quick, filling start to the day.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The burrito originated in Mexico in the early 20th century as a convenient way to carry food on the go.
The combination of eggs and bacon makes the dish high in protein and fat, providing long‑lasting satiety.
In the United States egg burritos are often served in fast‑food restaurants, but traditional recipes include fresh veggies and homemade sauces.
Traditional Mexican burritos usually omit cheese, whereas the American version almost always includes it.
Bacon in a burrito is typically smoked, giving the dish a distinctive aroma and crisp texture.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs and bacon provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair and sustained energy.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, while bacon adds niacin and riboflavin, both important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Bacon and whole‑grain tortillas contribute a modest amount of iron, needed for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Nutrient‑dense vegetables
items.content: Added tomatoes, onions, and peppers supply vitamin C and antioxidants.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The mix of protein, fat, and carbohydrates helps keep you full longer.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Bacon is high in saturated fat, so people with cardiovascular concerns should limit intake.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Bacon is often salty; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to eggs must avoid this dish.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Egg burrito with bacon is relatively high in calories, so portion control is advised for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The burrito is usually served hot. Warm it in the microwave or on a skillet, cut it in half, and eat with your hands. Add fresh salsa, guacamole, or sour cream to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Refrigerate a prepared burrito in an airtight container for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 1 month. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Fava beans (also known as broad beans) are a legume native to the Mediterranean, North Africa and parts of Asia. Cooked fava beans have a mild, slightly nutty flavor and a tender yet firm texture. They are used in salads, spreads, soups, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fava beans are also called "broad beans" or "horse beans" in different regions.
In ancient Greek mythology fava symbolized fertility and abundance.
The seeds are protein‑rich, containing up to 26 % protein by dry weight.
In Italy, a traditional dish called "fave" is a simple puree of cooked fava beans.
Their dense texture makes them a popular meat substitute in vegetarian recipes.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Cooked fava beans provide about 7 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Fava beans supply folate, thiamine and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals: iron and magnesium
items.content: Iron supports oxygen transport, while magnesium is essential for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Fava beans raise blood glucose slowly, making them suitable for blood‑sugar management.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fava beans, ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and cooking help lower its level.

items.title: Raw bean toxins
items.content: Raw fava beans contain lectins that can be toxic; thorough cooking eliminates them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook fava beans in salted water for 20‑30 minutes, then add them to salads, pastas, soups, or mash them into a spread. They pair well with olive oil, lemon, garlic, and fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked fava beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Discard any beans with off‑odors or signs of spoilage.

multiple-meat-sandwich-on-white.title: Multiple Meat Sandwich on White Bread

content.title: About
content.content: The Multiple Meat Sandwich on White Bread (1855) is a hearty sandwich made with thin slices of beef, ham, chicken breast, and sausage layered between two slices of soft white bread. It is typically served with lettuce, tomato, and a light sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original 1855 recipe used only three meats: beef, ham, and chicken.
White bread in this sandwich is traditionally baked without seeds to let the meat flavors shine.
The sandwich is a common quick lunch option in school cafeterias.
Some regions add a slice of smoked bacon for extra aroma.
The product name comes from the menu code 1855 used by a large café chain.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Multiple meat types provide essential amino acids for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef and chicken breast are rich in heme iron, which is readily absorbed.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat supplies B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Balanced carbohydrates
items.content: White bread offers a quick source of glucose for immediate energy.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Added lettuce and tomato increase dietary fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed meats like ham and sausage can be salty, which may affect people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Certain meats, especially sausage, contain saturated fats that should be limited.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rare individuals may experience allergic reactions to specific meat proteins.

items.title: Gluten in bread
items.content: White bread contains gluten, making the sandwich unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is easy to eat by hand, preferably cut in half. Serve with mustard, mayo, or a light yogurt sauce. For a fresher taste, add cucumber, radish, or extra lettuce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for no more than 24 hours. For longer storage, separate the components: store meat in an airtight container, keep bread in a dry place, and keep vegetables in a separate bag.
